anchor_text: Live regist'red upon our brazen tombs
summary: 'Brazen' means made of brass or bronze. Brass memorial plaques set into church floors and walls were the standard monumental inscription of the era — a way for the famous to survive in public memory after death. Navarre means that fame will be literally engraved on their grave-markers.

anchor_text: cormorant devouring Time
summary: A cormorant is a seabird notorious for its voracious appetite; to call Time 'cormorant' is to make it a personified monster that consumes everything. The phrase is a compressed metaphor comparing the destructive passage of time to a gluttonous bird that swallows its catch whole.
detail: Personified Time as a devouring force — armed with a scythe ('scythe's keen edge,' TLN 6) — was a Renaissance commonplace going back to Ovid's 'Tempus edax rerum' ('Time the devourer of things,' Metamorphoses 15.234). Shakespeare stacks the imagery: Time is both the famished cormorant and the Death-figure with a scythe. The king's speech is itself a catalogue of rhetorical figures — personification, paradox ('disgrace of death' = honour through the disgrace of dying), and the Petrarchan trope of literary fame outlasting mortality.

The cormorant as a figure for voracious consumption is a Shakespearean commonplace, and the Ovid 'Tempus edax rerum' parallel is entirely mainstream; stacking the scythe image (TLN 6) is confirmed by the text.

anchor_text: our court shall be a little academe
summary: An 'academe' is an academy for learning, named after the Athenian grove where Plato taught (the Academia). Navarre is proposing that his court become a miniature Platonic school of philosophy and contemplative study.
detail: The Platonic Academy in Athens met in a grove sacred to the hero Academus, giving Western European universities and learned societies their name. Renaissance 'academies' — formal clubs of scholars and noblemen devoted to philosophy, poetry, and debate — flourished across Italy and France; Navarre's proposal glances at this fashionable intellectual movement. The play's first scene stages the instant collapse of the idealistic project: the oaths are barely signed before Berowne finds them absurd and the French princess's embassy makes them unkeepable.

anchor_text: Fat paunches have lean pates; and dainty bits Make rich the ribs, but bankrupt quite the wits
summary: Longaville delivers a neat antithetical proverb: overeating ('fat paunches,' 'dainty bits') fattens the body but empties the mind. The couplet works by balance and opposition — body vs. mind, wealth vs. bankruptcy — and was a standard Renaissance argument for fasting as an aid to study.
detail: The sentiment echoes classical praise of frugality as necessary for intellectual work; Cicero and Seneca both argue that the sated body dulls the intellect. In medical terms, Tudor physiology held that gluttony thickened the animal spirits, making them sluggish and unfit for thought. Longaville's rhyming couplet is also a miniature performance of wit — he instantly converts the oath into an epigram, the currency of the courtly intellectual world the play is satirizing.

anchor_text: By yea and nay, sir, then I swore in jest
summary: 'By yea and nay' is a mild oath that swears by nothing more than the plain words 'yes' and 'no.' It echoes Christ's command in Matthew 5:37, 'let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay,' which teaches that an honest man's bare word should suffice and condemns elaborate swearing. Costard uses the phrase as a light, throwaway oath to insist his word is to be taken seriously without ceremony, then immediately wriggles out of it ('then I swore in jest').

anchor_text: Light, seeking light, doth light of light beguile
summary: This line uses polyptoton — the same word ('light') repeated with different meanings in quick succession: the light of the scholar's eye, the light of knowledge or truth, sight itself, and natural daylight. Berowne's point is that straining the eyes to read by candlelight damages the very faculty (eyesight) you are exercising.
detail: Four distinct senses of 'light' clash in a single line: (1) the scholar who is 'light-seeking' (seeking knowledge); (2) the light of truth he hunts; (3) the faculty of sight ('light of light beguile' = rob the eye of its seeing-power); (4) natural or candle light. The rhetorical device is polyptoton or antanaclasis — a favourite display of the euphuistic style Shakespeare is simultaneously deploying and parodying. Berowne argues that book-study by lamplight causes blindness, so paradoxically ruins the instrument of learning. The argument is absurdist but structurally impeccable, which is the point: Berowne can make any case sound compelling.

anchor_text: These earthly godfathers of heaven's lights That give a name to every fixed star
summary: Berowne mocks astronomers who catalogue and name the fixed stars — an allusion to Renaissance stellar catalogues. Naming stars, he argues, gives no more real knowledge of them than a godfather gains from naming a child at baptism. The 'godfathers' pun on the baptismal role, where a godfather bestows a name without thereby understanding the person.
detail: The major Renaissance star catalogues — Ptolemy's Almagest (in wide circulation), Copernicus's De Revolutionibus (1543), and Tycho Brahe's ongoing observations (published 1598, after LLL, but his fame was European) — named, numbered, and recorded the fixed stars as a cornerstone of astronomical learning. Berowne debunks the pursuit: labelling something is not the same as knowing it. The godfather analogy is also a dig at pedantry: a godfather 'names' the child he sponsors at baptism, yet the name confers no real acquaintance. The argument is part of Berowne's sustained satire of academic learning as superficial nomenclature.

anchor_text: for barbarism spoke more Than for that angel knowledge you can say
summary: 'Barbarism' means ignorance and the uncivilized condition — the opposite of learning. 'Angel knowledge' is knowledge so pure and exalted it belongs to angels, not mortals. Berowne admits he has been arguing for ignorance rather than for the angelic learning Navarre praised, yet he will keep his oath anyway.

The edict, Berowne says, is barbarous to both the class and the quality of women. The pun lets him mock Longaville's savage penalty as simultaneously socially outrageous and ungentlemanly.

anchor_text: Necessity will make us all forsworn Three thousand times within this three years' space; For every man with his affects is born, Not by might master'd, but by special grace
summary: Berowne sets out the theological and natural argument against the oath. 'Affects' means natural appetites and desires — feelings men are born with, not chosen. Mastering them requires not mere willpower ('might') but divine grace. The argument borrows the Protestant-Calvinist language of fallen human nature: without God's special grace, self-control is impossible.
detail: The phrase 'special grace' is specifically Calvinist in flavour: Reformed theology held that the natural man's will is too corrupted by the Fall to master sinful desire by its own strength; only God's freely given special grace can bring the will into obedience. Berowne uses this theological argument to mock Navarre's Stoic project — the humanist dream of self-perfection through discipline is, he implies, theologically naive. The speech plants the key word 'forsworn' (oath-broken), which recurs relentlessly across the play as each lord capitulates to love.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 149

The reading that 'special grace' is specifically Calvinist is plausible but over-specified: the phrase was part of common theological vocabulary across Catholic and Protestant traditions, not exclusively Reformed, and Berowne's argument here is naturalistic (men are born with appetites) rather than strictly Calvinist; the Romans 7:18 locus is a reasonable parallel but the annotation overstates the doctrinal precision.

anchor_text: Stands in attainder of eternal shame
summary: 'Attainder' is a legal term: the judgment by which a person convicted of a capital crime was declared 'attainted,' losing all civil rights, land, and even the right to transmit an inheritance. Here Berowne uses it figuratively: breaking the oath will 'attaint' the breaker with perpetual dishonour as surely as a criminal conviction.

anchor_text: refined traveller of Spain
summary: Armado, the 'refined traveller of Spain,' is a stock character type: the boastful Spanish soldier-courtier (miles gloriosus) transplanted to a French court. England's long wars and rivalry with Spain (the Armada of 1588 had come only a few years before) made the pompous, word-spinning Spaniard an immediately recognizable comic type for Shakespeare's audience.
detail: The miles gloriosus (braggart soldier) was a classical comic type from Plautus, but Shakespeare's Armado is a specifically Spanish variant: the Castilian hidalgo (gentleman) who combines military pretension with inflated rhetoric and threadbare poverty. The description 'mint of phrases in his brain' — a man who coins verbal currency of no real value — perfectly sketches the euphuist or Gongorist style associated with Spanish courtly prose. His name, Don Adriano de Armado, parodies the 'Armada' itself (the name means 'armed fleet' in Spanish). The description 'A man in all the world's new fashion planted' (164) marks him as a creature of fashionable novelty, which in the 1590s meant Spanish courtly affectation.

sources.name: Plautus, Miles Gloriosus

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 163

anchor_text: This child of fancy, that Armado hight
summary: 'Hight' is an archaic past tense meaning 'is named' or 'was called.' It was already old-fashioned in Shakespeare's day, surviving in literary use to give an antique, quasi-chivalric flavour — appropriate for the fantastical Armado. 'Child of fancy' means a creature of imagination and caprice.

anchor_text: A man of fire-new words, fashion's own knight
summary: 'Fire-new' means newly forged, fresh from the smith's fire — applied literally to metal straight from the furnace. Berowne uses it of Armado's vocabulary: his words are not old currency but freshly minted novelties, spanking-new coinages that gleam without having any proven value. 'Fashion's own knight' caps the satire: he is knighted by mere fashion, not by deeds.

anchor_text: I am his Grace's tharborough
summary: Dull means 'thirdborough,' a minor parish constable — a petty local officer responsible for keeping the peace, ranking below a headborough or chief constable. Dull's mangling of the word ('tharborough') is his first demonstration of the verbal confusion that makes him the play's emblem of oblivious dimness.
detail: A 'thirdborough' (sometimes 'tharborough,' a dialect form) was a subordinate constable in a parish — below a headborough, who was below the high constable. The title appears in the statutes of the peace. Dull's malapropism-like pronunciation 'tharborough' introduces the play's comic theme of language corrupted or misunderstood: where Armado inflates, Dull deflates. He also twice calls the King 'the duke' (181), which Berowne corrects without explanation, showing Dull's unfamiliarity with the title.

anchor_text: the contempts thereof are as touching me
summary: Costard means 'contents' — the contents of Armado's letter concern him. 'Contempts' is his malapropism (accidentally substituting a wrong word for the right one), but it also accidentally makes sense: the letter does treat him with contempt, so the misfire produces an unintended truth. This is Costard's characteristic mode of comic language.

anchor_text: manner and form following, sir; all those three: I was seen with her in the manor-house, sitting with her upon the form
summary: Costard runs a sustained pun on 'manner/manor' and 'form.' The legal phrase 'in manner and form' (used to introduce charges) means 'in the following way and shape.' Costard takes both words literally: 'manor' as the manor-house, 'form' as a bench. By literalizing the legal formula he simultaneously confesses the facts and turns the indictment into comedy.
detail: The legal phrase 'in manner and form following' was a standard formula in common-law pleading, signalling that the exact form of the charge was about to be stated. Costard pretends to take each legal abstraction ('manner' = way; 'form' = legal form) as a concrete noun ('manor' = country house; 'form' = wooden bench), and 'following' as the act of physically following Jaquenetta into the park. The triple pun performs the whole incident through wordplay alone and turns the solemn prosecution into a comedy of linguistic literalism — which is exactly what the play is doing at every level with the lords' oaths.

anchor_text: the welkin's vicegerent and sole dominator of Navarre, my soul's earth's god and body's fostering patron
summary: Armado's letter opens with a piling-up of extravagant honorifics. 'Welkin' is the sky or heavens; 'vicegerent' means deputy-ruler. Armado calls Navarre 'the sky's deputy' and then loads on more: 'sole dominator,' 'my soul's earth's god,' 'fostering patron.' This heaping of titles is deliberately preposterous — parody of the inflated rhetoric of formal addresses, the kind of thing real petitions and letters of the period opened with, pushed to absurdity.
detail: The style is euphuism taken to comic excess. John Lyly's prose romance Euphues (1578) had made elaborate ornamental rhetoric — balance, antithesis, alliteration, borrowed classical analogies — the fashionable style of the 1580s-90s; Armado's letter is a caricature of euphuism applied to an accusation against a peasant. 'Welkin' was already a slightly archaic poetic word for sky; pairing it with the Latinate 'vicegerent' ('one who exercises the authority of a superior') creates a comic mismatch of registers. The whole letter is Shakespeare mocking inflated official and courtly prose.

Euphuism as the satirical target of Armado's inflated salutation is the standard reading; 'welkin' (sky) + 'vicegerent' (deputy) as comic register-clash is well-supported, and the Lyly connection is mainstream LLL scholarship.

anchor_text: besieged with sable-coloured melancholy, I did commend the black-oppressing humour to the most wholesome physic of thy health-giving air
summary: Armado describes his mood in terms of Renaissance medical theory. 'Melancholy' was one of the four humours — black bile ('sable-coloured' = black) — whose excess caused depression, despondency, and obsession. Recommending a walk in fresh air to expel the 'black-oppressing humour' was standard medical advice. Armado parodies the style of learned medical self-diagnosis.

Armado translates this quite routine prescription into a cascade of ornate periphrasis: he does not say 'I was sad and went for a walk' but writes nine lines to say the same thing. anchor_text: The first and second cause will not serve my turn; the passado he respects not, the duello he regards not
summary: Armado thinks like a duelist. The 'first and second cause' refers to the formal justifications for a duel according to the fashionable Italian codes of honor: a 'cause' was the specific insult that entitled a gentleman to demand satisfaction. A 'passado' is a fencing term for a forward thrust. The 'duello' is the formal code of dueling rules. Armado is saying that the normal rules of a duellist's life — insult, challenge, fight — are useless against Love.
detail: Dueling codes (derived from Italian masters such as Vincentio Saviolo, who published his handbook in English in 1595) specified categories of insult ('the lie,' 'the retort courteous,' etc.) that created formal 'causes' requiring satisfaction. The 'passado' is a step-thrust; the 'duello' is the whole system of formal combat etiquette. Shakespeare mocks such hair-splitting codes elsewhere in Romeo and Juliet (Mercutio on Tybalt's Italian fencing mannerisms) and in As You Like It (Touchstone's catalogue of degrees of the lie). Armado dramatizes his helplessness by imagining Love as an opponent who refuses to follow any of the proper rules of honorable combat.

anchor_text: Assist me, some extemporal god of rime, for I am sure I shall turn sonneter
summary: Armado invokes an imaginary deity of on-the-spot (extemporal = improvised, off the cuff) verse to help him write love poetry. His vow to 'turn sonneter' and produce 'volumes in folio' is comic overstatement: love has reduced this blustering soldier to reaching for a pen. It is also a self-aware joke about the Elizabethan fashion for writing sonnet sequences to prove one's love.

'Sonnet' in this period could mean any short love poem, not necessarily the 14-line form; but 'volumes in folio' — the largest book format, used for serious works like the Bible or legal records — is deliberately absurd as the planned product of love-struck verse. The scene anticipates the entire play's central joke: these men of learning will all abandon their books for sonnets.

anchor_text: Aquitaine, a dowry for a queen
summary: Aquitaine is the large southwestern region of France (the modern Bordeaux wine country and the Dordogne). The plot of the scene turns on it: the King of France holds it as security against a debt of 100,000 crowns owed by Navarre. 'A dowry for a queen' signals its enormous value — historically it was indeed the dowry Eleanor of Aquitaine brought to the English crown in 1152.

Shakespeare's fictional debt-and-security plot compresses historical tensions between France and the small kingdom of Navarre (ruled in the 1580s by the Protestant Henri of Bourbon, later Henri IV of France) and the French crown. The topical shimmer of the Navarre-France relationship lent the comedy a contemporary edge for the 1594-95 audience, though the play is not a political allegory.

summary: A 'votary' is a person who has taken a vow, especially a religious one — a sworn devotee. The Princess is asking which lords have joined the King's oath of celibacy and study. 'Vow-fellows' is Shakespeare's coinage for companions bound together by the same vow.

anchor_text: A man of sovereign parts, he is esteem'd, / Well fitted in arts, glorious in arms
summary: 'Sovereign parts' means pre-eminent gifts and qualities. 'Fitted in arts' means accomplished in learning; 'glorious in arms' means distinguished in warfare. anchor_text: His eye begets occasion for his wit

anchor_text: Our Lady help my lord! he'll be forsworn
summary: 'Our Lady' is the Virgin Mary — a Catholic oath of exclamation. The oath against women and the Virgin's patronage of women are placed in ironic juxtaposition.

The King has just declared he 'hath sworn an oath' that keeps women out; the Princess immediately predicts he will violate it by letting her in. Her 'Our Lady' functions as both a throwaway exclamation and a pointed irony: the one female intercessor above all others is invoked on behalf of a man whose vow is about to be defeated by female presence.

anchor_text: sworn out house-keeping: / 'Tis deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord, / And sin to break it
summary: 'Sworn out house-keeping' means to have taken an oath that abolishes the normal duties of hospitality — a great household was expected to keep open, generous house. The figure is a formal dilemma (a choice between two equally bad options).

The rhetorical figure (a dilemma presenting two equally unacceptable horns) is itself a witty move — the Princess, forbidden to enter, uses argument as her entry-pass.

anchor_text: let it blood
summary: Rosaline prescribes 'letting blood' as the cure for Berowne's sick heart. Bloodletting — opening a vein to drain excess blood — was the standard medical treatment for almost every ailment in Elizabethan medicine, based on the theory that disease arose from an imbalance of the four bodily 'humours' (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile). Rosaline then offers to do it by pricking the heart with her eye.

Her follow-up ('Will you prick't with your eye?') is a bawdy double entendre: 'prick' is to pierce, but also carries a sexual sense, and 'eye' puns on French 'oui' (yes). Berowne's response ('No point, with my knife') continues the mock-combat: 'no point' (= certainly not) also puns on the sharp point of the lancet used for bloodletting. The whole exchange sustains a rapid wit-duel under the guise of medical banter.

anchor_text: Perchance light in the light
summary: Longaville asks about the lady 'in the white' (wearing a white dress or mask). Boyet jokes she is 'a woman sometimes, an you saw her in the light' — playing on 'light' as illumination. Boyet's 'a woman sometimes, an you saw her in the light' uses sense 1 to evade the question (she is a woman when you can see her clearly); Longaville's 'Perchance light in the light' deploys sense 3 (she might be loose in her morals, in the daylight). Boyet then refuses to name her publicly: 'She hath but one for herself; to desire that were a shame' — her name is her own property, and asking it is presumptuous.

anchor_text: My lips are no common, though several they be

anchor_text: the heart's still rhetoric disclosed with eyes
summary: Boyet describes the silent, involuntary eloquence of the King's gaze: the 'heart's still [silent] rhetoric' is the feeling the heart communicates without words, 'disclosed' (revealed, opened) through the eyes. Eyes as a medium of love-communication was a fundamental convention of Elizabethan love-poetry.

Boyet's elaborate account (TLN 680-693) of the King's involuntary love-symptoms — all senses 'lock'd in his eye,' heart 'like an agate' stamped with the Princess's image, tongue stumbling to keep up with the eye — is a set-piece of this tradition. anchor_text: 'The hobby-horse is forgot.'

anchor_text: by, in, and without, upon the instant

anchor_text: thy silly thought, my spleen; the heaving of my lungs provokes me to ridiculous smiling

anchor_text: This wimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy, This senior-junior, giant-dwarf, Dan Cupid
summary: Berowne piles up oxymorons and abusive epithets for Cupid, the Roman god of love: 'wimpled' (blindfolded), 'purblind' (nearly blind), 'senior-junior, giant-dwarf' (simultaneously ancient and infantile, all-powerful and tiny). 'Dan' is a title of respect (from Latin dominus, master), making 'Dan Cupid' an ironic 'Master Cupid.'

The oxymorons 'senior-junior, giant-dwarf' are Berowne at his most self-consciously rhetorical: the god who has governed human love since the beginning of time is also a screaming baby. 'Dan' (Latin dominus) appears in Chaucer as an honorific for learned or divine figures. Ovid's Metamorphoses 1.468-474 describes the golden and leaden arrows; the blind infant image was ubiquitous in Renaissance emblems and poetry.

anchor_text: Dread prince of plackets, king of codpieces, Sole imperator, and great general Of trotting 'paritors
summary: Berowne assigns Cupid sovereignty over the most intimate items of dress: a 'placket' was a slit in a petticoat or skirt (by extension, female genitalia); a 'codpiece' was the padded, often conspicuous pouch on men's breeches covering the groin. Together they make Cupid the lord of both sexes' private parts.

Cupid as 'general of trotting apparitors' means he is the supreme commander of all that causes people to end up in the sex courts. The string of titles — 'prince of plackets, king of codpieces, sole imperator, great general' — mirrors the swollen political rhetoric of Armado earlier in the scene, and turns both Elizabethan fashion and Elizabethan legal procedure into instruments of erotic comedy. anchor_text: A woman, that is like a German clock, Still a-repairing, ever out of frame
summary: German mechanical clocks were famously elaborate and unreliable in Elizabethan England — admired for their craft but constantly breaking down. Berowne's dismissal of Rosaline as 'like a German clock' says she is ornate, high-maintenance, always out of order, and can only work if constantly watched. The comparison is cruel wit rather than genuine feeling.

'Out of frame' means out of working order, out of joint (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'frame'). The pun on 'being watch'd... go right' — that a watch (timepiece) works only when watched — completes the conceit. That Berowne immediately contradicts this contemptuous portrait by listing Rosaline's charms (pitch-black eyes, lines 885-886) shows that the clock-speech is self-lacerating comedy, not real misogyny.

anchor_text: Though Argus were her eunuch and her guard
summary: Argus was a many-eyed giant from Greek myth, set by Juno to watch Io (a young woman Juno suspected of attracting Jupiter's attentions); with eyes covering his whole body he could watch without ever sleeping. Berowne implies Rosaline is so determined to act on her desires that even the unsleeping Argus could not keep her in check.

Argus became proverbially the image of a vigilant guard who still cannot prevent what he watches over.

anchor_text: a' show'd a mounting mind
summary: 'A'' is an Elizabethan shortened form of 'he.' 'Mounting mind' means an ambitious, aspiring spirit — someone eager to climb to the top, here literally and figuratively, since the rider spurred up a steep hill.

The Princess is watching what she suspects is the King of Navarre, and her observation is wryly political — the man sworn to academic withdrawal has ridden out energetically to hunt.

anchor_text: upon the edge of yonder coppice; A stand where you may make the fairest shoot
summary: A 'coppice' is a thicket of small trees cut back regularly to produce straight, usable poles. A 'stand' is a hunter's fixed position — a spot to wait motionless for game to pass. The Forester is directing the Princess to the best place to shoot deer as they break out of the wood.

The Princess is shooting with a bow from a stationary position, a fashionable pursuit for noblewomen. 'Fairest shoot' means 'best shot,' but the Princess immediately seizes on 'fair' and 'shoot' as compliments, launching the scene's wit-combat with the Forester.

anchor_text: I thank my beauty, I am fair that shoot
summary: The Princess turns the Forester's hunting term 'fairest shoot' into a compliment on her looks: 'fair' = beautiful, and 'that shoot' = who does the shooting. She then spins a small theological joke (line 917-918): 'my beauty will be sav'd by merit' mocks the Protestant doctrine that salvation is by faith alone, not by good works ('merit'). She is saying, with mock-piety, that a woman's beauty should 'save' her by its own intrinsic worth — 'heresy in fair.'

When the Princess says 'beauty will be sav'd by merit,' 'merit' alludes to the Catholic doctrine of salvation through meritorious works, which Protestants called heresy — hence 'O heresy in fair.' She flips the theological terms into a joke about feminine beauty and flattery: saying a woman is beautiful not because she deserves it but to gain a reward (money, which she just handed over) is both the 'heresy' of praising beauty 'beyond its worth' and a gibe at the Forester for hollow flattery.

anchor_text: you can carve; Break up this capon
summary: 'Carve' means to cut up food at table — a courtly skill, since carving was considered an art gentlemen should master. To 'break up' a capon (a castrated rooster fattened for eating) was the technical term for opening and portioning a fowl. The Princess is using poultry-carving slang to mean 'open this sealed letter' — a letter from Armado is compared to a fat, hollow bird.

'Carve' also carried connotations of complaisance — a man who 'carves' to a lady is obsequiously attentive — so the Princess is teasing Boyet as a smooth, obliging courtier. 'Break up' was the standard culinary phrase for opening a carcass at the breast (and separately for opening a sealed letter); Shakespeare doubles both uses here.

anchor_text: magnanimous and most illustrate king Cophetua set eye upon the pernicious and indubitate beggar Zenelophon
summary: King Cophetua was a legendary African king who, despite despising women, fell in love with a beggar-girl named Zenelophon and made her his queen. Armado is casting himself as Cophetua and Jaquenetta as Zenelophon. The joke is in the inflated language: 'magnanimous and most illustrate' (grand-spirited and illustrious) for the king, 'pernicious and indubitate' (harmful and undoubted) for the beggar-girl — absurd modifiers that parody the style of chivalric romance.
detail: The King Cophetua story appears in a popular Elizabethan ballad ('King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid'). Shakespeare alludes to it elsewhere (Romeo and Juliet 2.1, Richard II 5.3, 2 Henry IV 5.3). 'Magnanimous' and 'illustrate' (= illustrious) are Latinate terms appropriate to formal panegyric but comically misapplied to Armado's ridiculous position; 'pernicious' (harmful, wicked) is equally absurd as a word for a beggar girl. 'Indubitate' (undoubted, certain) is Armado coining an English word from Latin indubitatus. The whole sentence is a parody of inflated Euphuistic prose style — the fashionable, over-ornamented prose of John Lyly's Euphues (1578).

anchor_text: Veni, vidi, vici; which to anatomize in the vulgar
summary: 'Veni, vidi, vici' — Latin for 'I came, I saw, I conquered' — was Julius Caesar's famous report of his swift victory at the Battle of Zela (47 BCE), quoted by the ancient biographer Plutarch. Armado's letter borrows Caesar's words to describe King Cophetua falling in love with a beggar-girl, which reduces the most celebrated military dispatch of antiquity to a joke about romantic conquest. 'Anatomize in the vulgar' means 'explain in the common tongue' (i.e., English, not Latin).
detail: Suetonius also records the phrase (Julius 37). The comic effect depends on the audience knowing Caesar's terse, three-word triumphal report. Armado deploys it as high-sounding ammunition for the trivial claim that a king saw a beggar and fell in love; then, having used the Latin, he laboriously 'anatomizes' (dissects, explains) it for readers who might not know Latin — 'O base and obscure vulgar!' — in a parody of pedantic translation. The phrase also recurs in As You Like It (5.2), always as a boast.

The attribution to Caesar and the comic reduction of a famous military dispatch to a love-conquest is the obvious and correct reading; citing Plutarch as primary source is accurate (North's translation was the standard English text), and Suetonius as corroboration is sound.

anchor_text: Thus dost thou hear the Nemean lion roar 'Gainst thee, thou lamb
summary: The Nemean lion was a ferocious beast whose hide no weapon could pierce; strangling it was the first of the twelve labours of Hercules. Armado compares himself to this invincible monster ('the Nemean lion') roaring at the meek Jaquenetta ('thou lamb'), commanding her to submit or be devoured. The poem turns a love declaration into a mock-heroic threat.
detail: Armado's verse is a parody of the 'blazon' tradition in which the lover praises his mistress's beauty, here inverted: instead of praising Jaquenetta, Armado threatens her as a predator threatens prey. 'Repasture for his den' = food stored in his lair. The comic absurdity is that this overwhelming lion is Armado himself, a penniless, threadbare fantasist. Shakespeare uses the Nemean lion elsewhere for genuine heroic resolve (Hamlet 1.4: 'as hardy as the Nemean lion's nerve'), which makes Armado's self-casting all the more ludicrous. The image derives from Apollodorus's Library 2.5.1 and Ovid's account of Hercules' twelve labours.

anchor_text: A phantasime, a Monarcho, and one that makes sport
summary: A 'phantasime' (fantasm) is an extravagant fantasist, someone out of touch with reality. 'Monarcho' was the nickname of a real Italian eccentric in Elizabethan London — a deluded man who styled himself emperor of the world and was tolerated at court as a comic figure. Boyet is telling the Princess that Armado is a well-known type of court fool: a grandiose, self-important entertainer like that famous pretender.

anchor_text: My lady goes to kill horns; but, if thou marry, Hang me by the neck, if horns that year miscarry
summary: The Princess hunts deer — animals with literal horns. Boyet puns on the other meaning of 'horns': the cuckold's horns, which in folklore grew on a man whose wife was unfaithful. He jokingly bets that if Rosaline marries, her husband will grow cuckold's horns within the year.

Boyet's pun — a woman who kills real deer-horns will soon give her husband metaphorical ones — belongs to the scene's sustained archery-and-anatomy bawdy sequence. Rosaline's reply ('If we choose by the horns, yourself: come not near') turns the gibe back at Boyet, implying that he already has them. anchor_text: an old saying, that was a man when King Pepin of France was a little boy
summary: King Pepin (Pepin the Short, d. 768 CE) was the father of Charlemagne and the first Carolingian king of France — a figure so remote in time that 'since King Pepin's day' had become an Elizabethan phrase meaning 'since ancient times, time out of mind.' The joke is that neither proverb exists: they are inventing deliberately pompous, pseudo-ancient authorities for a trivial wager about who landed the better verbal blow. The names are chosen for maximum antiquity: Pepin (8th century) and Guinever (legendary, pre-historical) both signal 'this is the oldest possible saying.' The exchange also implicitly pairs France and Britain, the nations at the diplomatic centre of the play's plot.

anchor_text: A mark marvellous well shot; for they both did hit it
summary: The closing exchange between Boyet, Maria, and Costard is built on archery terms that all carry sexual double meanings. 'Mark' = a target, but also a female genitalia. 'Prick' = the central pin of an archery target, but also its anatomical double. 'Clout' = the white cloth at the target's centre (to 'hit the clout' = score a bull's-eye). 'Pin' = the pin that held the clout in place. 'Cleave the pin' = split the pin to score a perfect shot. The whole sequence is a parody of courtly wit turning obscene.
detail: Renaissance archery terminology offered an unusually rich vocabulary for sexual puns: 'mark,' 'prick,' 'clout,' 'pin,' 'shaft,' 'bow-hand.' Boyet, Maria, and Costard pass the terms back and forth, each capping the last, until Maria calls a halt ('you talk greasily; your lips grow foul'). Costard's final parting shot — 'She's too hard for you at pricks, sir; challenge her to bowl' — extends the bawdy from archery to bowls, where 'rubbing' (Boyet's 'I fear too much rubbing') is a technical term for the bias of the bowl against an obstruction (but also an obvious pun). The sequence demonstrates the play's obsession with wit as a form of sexual sparring.

anchor_text: most incony vulgar wit! When it comes so smoothly off, so obscenely
summary: 'Incony' (also spelled 'inkony') is an Elizabethan dialect word meaning delicate, fine, or exquisite — used here with comic affection. Costard, the clown, is praising the wit-combat he has just watched as exquisitely crude ('incony vulgar'): the combination of a refined term with 'vulgar' (common, coarse) is itself the joke. He then adds 'so obscenely' — clearly meaning something like 'so fittingly, so neatly,' not the modern sense, though the bawdy overtone is deliberate.
detail: The word 'incony' appears only three times in Shakespeare, all in LLL — where it marks Costard's half-comprehending admiration for the courtiers' play. Its dialectal origin (probably northern English) makes it slightly outlandish in a courtly context, adding to the comedy. 'Obscenely' in Elizabethan use could mean both 'indecently' and 'neatly, fittingly'; Costard's mixed register — dialect term plus Latin-derived word in praise of dirty wordplay — perfectly captures his social position as an appreciative outsider.

anchor_text: I will something affect the letter; for it argues facility
summary: Holofernes announces he will 'affect the letter' — meaning he will use alliteration. He then produces a doggerel epitaph in which nearly every stressed word starts with the same consonant: 'The preyful Princess pierc'd and prick'd a pretty pleasing pricket.' The piling up of P-words is 'paroemion' or extreme alliteration, a recognised rhetorical device that was considered crude when overdone. 'It argues facility' means it shows he can do it effortlessly.
detail: Extreme alliteration was a feature of Anglo-Saxon verse and of the early Tudor 'aureate' style; by the 1590s educated readers mocked it as a sign of provincial or old-fashioned writing — the schoolmaster-poet who has learned the rule without the taste to know when to stop. Shakespeare has already parodied this in A Midsummer Night's Dream with the mechanicals' 'Pyramus' prologue ('Whereat with blade, with bloody, blameful blade'). Holofernes's extemporal p-poem is the same joke: the more conscientious his alliteration, the worse the poem.

anchor_text: Some say a sore; but not a sore till now made sore with shooting

Holofernes's epigram multiplies these terms and adds the arithmetic conceit that the letter L, Roman numeral for 50, converts 'sore' into 'sorel' — producing 'fifty sores one sorel.' The entire exercise is comic pedantry: technical knowledge deployed without practical point, and the more laborious the pun, the funnier it is.

anchor_text: ventricle of memory, nourished in the womb of pia mater
summary: Holofernes describes his poetic inspiration in the language of Renaissance brain anatomy. The 'ventricles' of the brain were three hollow chambers believed to house the mental faculties: the front ventricle (imagination), the middle (reason), and the rear (memory). The 'pia mater' is the thin, delicate membrane covering the brain — the innermost of three layers — whose name is Latin for 'tender mother.' Holofernes claims his creativity gestates there like a baby.

The three-ventricle brain theory was standard in university learning and grammar-school reading. Shakespeare uses 'pia mater' elsewhere for the brain or seat of thought (Twelfth Night 1.5: 'lemon-coloured stockings... crush a pia mater of no more brain than a stone'). The effect here is that Holofernes describes improvising a bad deer-pun in the grandest possible physiological terms.

anchor_text: Master parson, quasi pers-on. And if one should be pierced, which is the one?

anchor_text: good old Mantuan. I may speak of thee as the traveller doth of Venice

When Armado in Act 1 quotes Horace and Holofernes here quotes Mantuanus, Shakespeare is precisely targeting the very books his audience had been drilled on. anchor_text: Thy eye Jove's lightning bears, thy voice his dreadful thunder
summary: Berowne's sonnet to Rosaline compares her eyes to Jupiter's ('Jove's') lightning and her voice to his thunder. Jove (Jupiter) was the king of the Roman gods, and his traditional weapons were the thunderbolt and lightning. This is a standard Renaissance love-poetry hyperbole: to praise a woman's eyes by linking them to the most powerful force in classical heaven. The compliment carries more weight because Berowne is supposed to be sworn off women and their power.

By the 1590s the image was so conventional that its presence in Berowne's sonnet is precisely what Holofernes will mock as containing 'only numbers ratified' — metrically competent but poetically unoriginal. The sonnet belongs to the wider pattern in the play of the lords breaking their oath of study to write poems that are, by Holofernes's lights, technically adequate but imaginatively empty.

anchor_text: golden cadence of poesy, caret. Ovidius Naso was the man: and why, indeed, Naso but for smelling out the odoriferous flowers of fancy
summary: Holofernes pronounces Berowne's sonnet technically competent in metre ('numbers ratified') but lacking 'golden cadence' — i.e., true poetic grace. 'Caret' is Latin for 'it is lacking.' He then declares that Ovid ('Ovidius Naso') was the true poet — and then puns on Ovid's cognomen 'Naso,' which is Latin for 'nose': Ovid had a nose for sniffing out ('smelling out') the 'odoriferous flowers of fancy.' The pun is elaborate, ridiculous, and entirely characteristic of Holofernes.
detail: Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BCE-17 CE) was the Roman love poet whose Metamorphoses, Amores, and Ars Amatoria made him the presiding classical spirit of Renaissance erotic verse and myth. 'Naso' as a cognomen literally meant 'the one with the big nose' in Latin. Holofernes's pun — Ovid was the man for 'smelling' out poetic fancy because his name means nose — is the scene's most sustained example of his word-game pedantry: learned, technically clever, and entirely without point. The rejection of mere 'imitari' (imitation) that follows ('so doth the hound his master, the ape his keeper') is also characteristic: Holofernes values originality but demonstrates none.

anchor_text: I am coursing myself: they have pitched a toil

anchor_text: O! rimes are guards on wanton Cupid's hose: Disfigure not his slop

anchor_text: Vows are but breath, and breath a vapour is: Then thou, fair sun, which on my earth dost shine, Exhal'st this vapour-vow

anchor_text: sharp and sententious; pleasant without scurrility, witty without affection
summary: Nathaniel's praise strings together balanced pairs — 'sharp and sententious,' 'pleasant without scurrility,' 'witty without affection' — in a figure called antitheton (assertion followed by its negative counterpart). anchor_text: Bone? bone for bene: Priscian a little scratch'd
summary: Nathaniel says 'bone intelligo' ('I understand well/good') using 'bone' (French-influenced or simply wrong) instead of the correct Latin 'bene.' Holofernes corrects him: 'Priscian a little scratch'd.' Priscian was the great grammarian of late antiquity whose Institutiones Grammaticae was the standard Latin grammar text in medieval and Renaissance schools; to 'break' or 'scratch' Priscian's head was a proverbial expression for making a grammatical error.

Priscianus of Caesarea (fl. c. 500 CE) wrote the Institutiones Grammaticae, the most authoritative Latin grammar of the medieval and early modern period, used in virtually every Tudor grammar school. Holofernes's correction is gentle ('a little scratch'd... 'twill serve') — he cannot bring himself to humiliate his only admirer. The irony is that the pedant who just castigated Armado's improper Latin shows this small tolerance for his clergyman friend's solecism.

anchor_text: great feast of languages and stolen the scraps
summary: Moth and Costard mock the pedants from the side: they have feasted on language but only stolen the scraps — leftover Latin tags and borrowed phrases rather than genuine learning. It is a sharp image for the gap between the schoolroom's show of learning and real understanding, and the two servants voice what the audience is thinking.

Both images position Holofernes and Nathaniel as parasites on real intellectual culture, surviving on borrowed leftovers rather than generating their own thought. This is the play's recurring satirical argument: genuine wit (exemplified by Berowne, Rosalind, Moth) is distinguished from performed learning (the pedants, the affected lords) throughout. The pair's commentary functions as a choric correction, grounding the high-flown latinism in plain common sense.

anchor_text: honorificabilitudinitatibus
summary: This 27-letter Latin word (meaning 'the state of being able to be honoured') was a famous example of an absurdly long word, cited in medieval grammar exercises as the longest word in the Latin language. Costard uses it as a comic unit of measurement: the page Moth is shorter in height than this word is in letters. The joke is that Holofernes and Nathaniel have been talking about words so long that a word becomes a ruler.
detail: The word is the ablative plural of 'honorificabilitudinitas,' a medieval Latin coinage built from layers of nominal suffixes on 'honor.' It appears in Dante's De Vulgari Eloquentia (II.7) as an example of an unusually long Latin form, and in medieval pedagogical Latin as a schoolroom curiosity. It circulated widely in Tudor England as a joke-word, and its appearance here is both a display of Costard's unexpected awareness and a piece of theatrical wit pointing at the play's central theme: language inflated to the point of meaninglessness. Later (17th c.) it became notorious as a supposed Baconian cipher, but that reading is entirely without basis.

anchor_text: easier swallowed than a flap-dragon
summary: A 'flapdraon' (or snapdragon) was a party game in which raisins or small objects were floated in burning brandy; the player had to snatch one from the flame and swallow it quickly. It was a test of quickness and nerve. Costard says the tiny page Moth would be easier to swallow whole than one of these flaming morsels — a vivid insult to Moth's small size.
detail: The game was popular in Elizabethan taverns and houses at Christmas and harvest celebrations; Falstaff is said to have 'drunk candles' ends with Mistress Quickly and 'eat a whole supper of sack-posset and flapdragons' (Henry V 2.3). The image heightens Costard's mock-praise of Moth by making him tinier even than a flaming raisin. It also continues the comic competition between Costard and Moth that runs through the scene: Costard is the 'natural' clown who wins rhetorical points against the professional wit by virtue of his sheer simplicity.

anchor_text: he teaches boys the hornbook. What is a, b, spelt backward with the horn on his head?
summary: The hornbook was the first literacy tool given to young children: a single sheet bearing the alphabet and the Lord's Prayer, mounted on a wooden board and protected by a thin sheet of transparent horn. Moth's question — what is 'b' backward with a horn added? — is a riddling setup: 'b' backward is nothing written, but the answer aimed at is 'Ba' (line 1635), the sound a sheep makes. A man with a horn is a cuckold. The whole passage strings together jokes about cuckoldry and stupidity at Holofernes's expense.
detail: The hornbook (a child's primer) sets up the pun: the 'horn' protecting its letters links to the horn the cuckold traditionally 'wears' (an invisible pair of horns, the sign that his wife has been unfaithful). 'Ba, pueritia' (Ba, childishness) — Holofernes sees only the sheep. The audience hears 'Ba' as both the sheep's bleat and the label for the horned cuckold Moth has just drawn. The vowel-game that follows ('a, e, i, o, u') ends with Moth pointing out that the sheep-sound ('o, u') finishes the word for the animal — meaning a ram (a horned beast), and punning on 'ou' as a French intensifier or as the horned creature completing the cuckold's portrait. The sexual undercurrent of horn/cuckold runs through the entire scene and surfaces again when Moth suggests using Holofernes's 'horn' to make a 'gig' (a spinning top) and 'whip about your infamy circum circa' (line 1650).

anchor_text: I smell false Latin! 'dunghill' for unguem
summary: Costard mangles a common Latin phrase: 'ad unguem' ('to the fingernail,' meaning perfectly or precisely — the craftsman's test of a smooth surface by running a fingernail across it) was a Horatian tag for 'to a nicety.' Costard replaces 'unguem' with 'dunghill,' producing 'ad dunghill' — a perfect comic deformation of learning. Holofernes is horrified to hear his Latin idiom turned to muck.

It was a school commonplace — the very kind of phrase that a grammar-school boy like Costard might have heard and distorted. The joke depends on the audience recognising the correct phrase while hearing the substitution; Holofernes's outrage ('I smell false Latin!') treats the deformation as a moral offence, exactly calibrated to his pedantic priorities. It also caps the scene's running joke: the two pedants' elaborate Latin is indistinguishable in function from Costard's 'ad dunghill' — all of them are performing rather than communicating.

anchor_text: you shall present before her the Nine Worthies
summary: The Nine Worthies were a standard medieval and Tudor set of nine model heroes of chivalry — three pagan (Hector, Alexander, Caesar), three biblical (Joshua, David, Judas Maccabaeus), and three Christian (Arthur, Charlemagne, Godfrey of Bouillon). Staged in pageants and civic shows across Europe, they embodied the ideals of military honour. Holofernes's casting — Nathaniel as Alexander, himself as 'Alexander,' this swain as Pompey, Moth as the infant Hercules — mangles the canonical list even before the pageant begins.
detail: Pompey is not one of the canonical Nine (he is Roman but not among the three pagan slots, filled by Hector, Alexander, and Caesar). Holofernes is already improvising freely, and his small troupe cannot supply nine actors for nine roles; he plans to 'play three myself.' The result in 5.2 is a pageant of only five Worthies (Joshua, Alexander, Judas Maccabaeus, Pompey, Hercules), heckled apart by the lords. The Worthies were familiar from pageant-books, school shows, and civic entertainments; the conceit of an amateur troupe botching them is close to the mechanicals' 'Pyramus and Thisbe' in A Midsummer Night's Dream (composed at roughly the same time).

anchor_text: if this fadge not, an antic
summary: 'Fadge' means to fit, suit, or succeed; 'if this fadge not' means 'if this does not work out.' Armado's contingency plan — a cruder, more obviously theatrical backup for the Worthies — reveals his pragmatism beneath the grand rhetoric: he is, at bottom, an entertainer who needs the show to please.

anchor_text: play on the tabor to the Worthies, and let them dance the hay
summary: A 'tabor' is a small drum, often played one-handed alongside a three-holed pipe by the same musician — the standard instrument for country dancing and rustic festivity. The 'hay' (also 'hey') was a lively winding country dance, resembling a reel. Dull, having understood nothing all scene, offers to contribute what he actually can do: keep a beat and call a dance. The joke is that his one competence is precisely the opposite of what the pedants have been doing — honest physical performance instead of verbal display.

The hay was a well-known country dance in which the performers wove in and out in a snaking chain — 'heigh' may be an imitation of the cry used to begin it. Dull's proposal to do the opposite of speaking — to play and dance — closes the scene with a reminder that there are forms of performance untouched by the pedants' word-disease. His final silent presence throughout the scene, capped by 'Nor understood none neither, sir,' is the play's bluntest comment on the scene's verbal excess.

anchor_text: A jest's prosperity lies in the ear Of him that hears it, never in the tongue Of him that makes it
summary: Rosaline states the play's most important truth about wit: a joke is only as good as its audience. The 'prosperity' (success, flourishing) of a jest belongs to the hearer, not the teller. anchor_text: Our wooing doth not end like an old play: Jack hath not Jill
summary: Berowne self-consciously announces that this comedy will not end the conventional way: in the 'old play' format (as in the standard comic ending) 'Jack gets Jill' — the hero wins the girl. The lords have not won their ladies. Shakespeare steps outside the play's own genre-conventions to comment on them, making Love's Labour's Lost the most formally self-aware of his comedies.

anchor_text: I am a votary: I have vowed to Jaquenetta to hold the plough for her sweet love three yeasr
summary: A 'votary' is a person bound by a vow — usually a religious vow, as a monk or nun is a votary of God. Armado applies the word to his comic love-vow to Jaquenetta, pledging to 'hold the plough' (do agricultural labor) for three years. The comedy is that the grandiloquent Spanish braggart, who has spent the play inflating himself with epic posture, ends by committing to farm work — brought down to earth by real love and real pregnancy.
detail: The word 'votary' echoes back to the play's opening: the King and his lords are 'votaries' to the academe (1.1). The parallel is sharp — the lords' academic vow is dissolved, while Armado, the play's buffoon, keeps his vow by doing precisely the unglamorous, unkingly thing the lords refuse. It is one of the play's quiet reversals: the comic figure acts with more consistency than the 'worthies.'

sources.name: OED

anchor_text: This side is Hiems, Winter; this Ver, the Spring
summary: The play ends with a 'dialogue' (debate) between Spring (Latin Ver) and Winter (Latin Hiems) — an academic genre called 'conflictus' or 'débat' going back to medieval Latin poetry and ultimately to classical eclogues. The two seasons argue their merits through their representatives' songs, with no clear winner. The form is borrowed from Renaissance school exercises and debates.
detail: The seasonal dialogue or conflictus was a common form in medieval Latin academic poetry (spring vs. winter, body vs. soul, water vs. wine). Armado's announcement — 'This side is Hiems, Winter; this Ver, the Spring; the one maintained by the owl, the other by the cuckoo' — frames it as a debating exercise, which aligns with the play's academic setting. The cuckoo (spring) and the owl (winter) were standard birds for their seasons in English poetry; the specific moral charge is that the cuckoo's song warns of cuckoldry, while the owl sings in cold, honest nights.

sources.name: Raby, A History of Secular Latin Poetry
sources.citation: F.J.E. Raby, A History of Secular Latin Poetry in the Middle Ages (1934), on the conflictus or débat genre: seasonal debates in medieval Latin verse.

The conflictus / débat as a medieval Latin academic genre for seasonal debate is correctly identified; the cuckoo/owl as standard season-birds in English poetry is accurate; the frame that this is an academic exercise fitting the play's setting is appropriate.

anchor_text: The cuckoo then on every tree Mocks married men, for thus sings he, Cuckoo
summary: The cuckoo's call sounded like the word 'cuckold' to Elizabethan ears ('cuckoo' / 'cuckold'), so its spring song was heard as a taunt to married men whose wives might be unfaithful. The Spring song begins with pastoral beauty but ends with this dark note: spring, the season of new love and new life, also brings the fear of infidelity.
detail: A 'cuckold' is a man whose wife is unfaithful; the word comes from 'cuckoo' because the cuckoo lays its eggs in other birds' nests, much as an adulterer usurps another man's household. The cuckoo-as-cuckold was a very old pun, well established in English folk tradition and Elizabethan comedy. The Spring song thus ends every verse with a word of ambiguous warning: spring's joy contains anxiety for husbands — a perfect ironic close for a play whose lords have been trying to win ladies while breaking their oaths.

The cuckoo/cuckold pun is well attested and proverbial in Elizabethan English; the etymology (cuckoo lays in other birds' nests → cuckold) is correct; the reading that the Spring song ends with dark irony appropriate to the play's oath-breaking theme is defensible.

anchor_text: When icicles hang by the wall, And Dick the shepherd blows his nail
summary: The Winter song is famous for its series of concrete, low-life domestic images — icicles, a shepherd warming his hands (blowing on his nails for heat), logs carried in, frozen milk, the parson's sermon drowned by coughing, a red-nosed Marian, crabs hissing in the bowl, and greasy Joan stirring the pot. It anchors the play's flight of wit in the actual world of cold, ordinary, un-courtly life.
detail: 'Dick the shepherd blows his nail' — to 'blow one's nail' means to blow on cold hands for warmth; it was a proverbial image of idle poverty. 'Merry note' (the owl's call) is ironic — it is harsh and cold. 'Greasy Joan doth keel the pot' — 'keel' means to skim or cool (the pot, by stirring), and 'greasy Joan' is a kitchen-woman with fat hands; 'roasted crabs' are crab-apples hissing in hot ale (a warming drink, 'lamb's wool'). The Winter song presents the real England — not the word-games of Navarre's court — as the final image.

anchor_text: The words of Mercury are harsh after the songs of Apollo
summary: Armado delivers the play's famous closing line: Mercury (god of speech, commerce, cunning, and messages) speaks harsh prose, while Apollo (god of music, poetry, and the sun) sings. The play's world of wordplay, debate, and courtly posturing (Mercury) must give way to the songs — the pure music of Spring and Winter that close the play. The line also gestures at the gap between words and the things they try to describe.

Apollo as god of music and song: Hesiod, Theogony 94-95 ('from the Muses and far-shooting Apollo are men singers').
